 6             This case is a New Mexico Future Test Year rate case. The Public Utility

 7   Act states that the Commission “shall set rates based on a test period that the

 8   commission determines best reflects the conditions to be experienced during the

 9   period when the rates determined by the commission take effect. If a future

10   test period is proposed, the commission shall give due consideration that the future

11   test period may best reflect those conditions.” 1 SPS has filed an FTY case because

12   the rates set in this case should reflect the costs SPS will incur, the loads SPS will

13   serve, and the system conditions SPS expects during the period when new rates are

14   in effect. If the Commission uses FTY costs but historical allocation factors, the

15   revenue requirement will not be assigned to the jurisdictions or the customer classes

16   based on the same period used to set the revenue requirement. This would violate

17   both the PUA and the matching principle that underlies cost-of-service ratemaking.

1         IV.     COMMISSION STANDARDS FOR APPROVING STIPULATIONS

2    Q.         Does the Commission have a rule regarding contested stipulations?

 3   A.         Yes. Rule 1.2.2.20(B) New Mexico Administrative Code (“NMAC”) governs

 4              contested stipulations, like the stipulation in this case. Subsection (B)(3) of that

5               rule states that “the commission or presiding officer shall schedule the stipulation

6               for public hearing and review unless it is determined that the nature and extent of

7               the opposition is such that hearing the stipulation will not materially conserve

 8              commission, staff, and party resources.” Subsection (B)(4) provides, “the

 9              proponents of the stipulation have the burden of supporting the stipulation with

10              sufficient evidence and legal argument to allow the Commission to approve it.”

11   Q.         Does the Commission have a stated policy regarding stipulations?

12   A.         Yes. The Commission has stated that it favors “the settlement of disputes to avoid

13              costly and protracted litigation” and recognizes that “a cooperative approach may

14              be more effective in reconciling the interest of all the parties than would the

 5   A.       Yes. Stipulations must be fair, just, and reasonable. 4 When evaluating stipulations,

 6            the Commission has applied the following criteria: 5
